And right now, I am staying in an overseas hotel where there is noise at night. As a result, I wake up to sounds during the night and then find myself unable to fall back asleep.

To deal with this, I once tried using Bose noise-canceling earphones to get by. The effect of the Bose noise canceling itself was extremely high, and no matter how much noise there was (at the time, there was a street performance going on until late at night, and the bass was so heavy it made the glass vibrate), I was able to sleep. The most troublesome part of traveling is finding a place to stay. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, and with the increase in inbound tourism, hotels in Japan have become crowded, making advance reservations essential.
Recently, I have been carefully selecting accommodations by comparing prices and conditions using hotel websites or booking platforms like Rakuten Travel and Booking.com.

Japanese accommodations generally offer a good balance between price and service. The going rate is 5,000 to 9,000 yen for a guesthouse, 6,000 to 10,000 yen for a business hotel, and 12,000 to 20,000 yen for a ryokan. I have traveled all over Japan and stayed in many hotels, ryokans, and guesthouses. As I have gained experience, I have become able to estimate the approximate cost of a stay based on the exterior, room facilities, and the content of the meals.

However, when the bill at checkout differs significantly from that expectation, I often feel quite disappointed. When I feel that 'this is definitely too expensive no matter how you look at it,' a lingering sense of dissatisfaction remains in my heart, and I end up thinking, 'I will never stay at this inn again!'

A few years ago, I stayed at a privately owned inn I found in a regional city. It had a stylish exterior, and my first impression was not bad, but the room was very ordinary and the bathroom was shared. Dinner and breakfast were included, but the food was nothing special.
